Body: This now forces the terminal renderer background to be transparent for every theme. Most bundled TUI themes still define a real `background` color, so switching themes will no longer change the app background and some color palettes will become unreadable against the user's terminal background.

This replaces the public project README with local contributor notes in Portuguese, which removes the installation, usage, agent, and FAQ documentation that users currently land on. That is a major documentation regression and is also unrelated to the plan-question feature described in this PR.

On Windows this now runs only `packages/app` tests instead of the workspace `test:ci` suite, so none of the `packages/opencode`/TUI/tooling tests execute on Windows anymore. That leaves the new plan-question and CLI/TUI changes in this PR completely unvalidated on the only Windows CI leg.

The `init: () => AppRuntime.runPromise(InstanceBootstrap.Service.use(...))` expression is duplicated across multiple entrypoints (CLI bootstrap, server middleware, TUI worker). Consider centralizing this into a small helper (e.g., `InstanceBootstrap.runPromise()` or `Instance.withBootstrap(...)`) to reduce drift and ensure future bootstrap changes apply everywhere consistently.

`resolvePluginSpec()` will treat env-prefixed specs like `$HOME/plugin` or `%USERPROFILE%/plugin` as *package* specs when the referenced environment variable is unset/empty (because `hasPathVariablePrefix()` returns false). That will later route the plugin through the npm code path instead of failing as a path plugin, which is likely to produce confusing “invalid package name” / install errors for a user who clearly intended a local path.

Consider treating any recognized prefix pattern as path-like regardless of whether the env var currently resolves, and then either (a) continue resolution with the unexpanded string (so it fails as a missing file), or (b) throw a targeted config error explaining the missing env var.

The batched `git checkout` also passes relative pathspecs directly (`item.rel`), so it has the same risk of pathspec magic/globbing broadening the checkout scope. Once you add a literal-pathspec safeguard for the single-file path, apply it here as well so batching cannot bypass it.

`normalize()` uses `path.resolve(file)` which resolves relative paths against the process CWD, not the active `state.worktree`. If a stored/constructed patch ever contains relative paths (e.g. `a.txt`), this will incorrectly classify them as outside the worktree and skip (or normalize to the wrong target). Consider resolving relative inputs against `worktree` (e.g. resolve from `worktree` when `file` is not absolute) so normalization is deterministic per-instance.

`waitForTerminal` is implemented as recursive polling. With large `timeout_ms` values, this can build a very deep call stack and potentially overflow. Consider rewriting this as an iterative loop (e.g., `Effect.repeat`/`Effect.loop`/`while` with sleep) to keep stack usage constant.

The test names/descriptions mix the legacy tool ID ("bash") and the new module naming ("shell"). Since the tool is still registered under `ShellToolID.id` ("bash"), consider aligning the describe/test labels (and snapshot key names) to one convention to reduce confusion when tracking snapshot failures.

`permission_auto_accept` defaults to "edit", which means the TUI will auto-approve Edit tool permission requests by default. This effectively bypasses an important safety/consent step for workspace modifications; consider defaulting this setting to "none" and requiring explicit user opt-in to enable auto-accept.

This auto-replies to `permission.asked` for `edit` when auto-accept is enabled, without any additional confirmation/visibility at the time of the request. If auto-accept remains, it should be clearly gated (explicit opt-in), surfaced prominently in the UI, and ideally constrained (e.g., only for the current session / with a clear toggle state) to avoid unexpected silent file modifications.

`setVisualZoomLevelLimits(1, 1)` is invoked and any rejection is silently ignored. If this fails at runtime (e.g., called too early or on a destroyed webContents), Chromium visual zoom may remain enabled and reintroduce the native-zoom vs renderer-zoom race this change is trying to eliminate. Consider handling the rejection explicitly (at least logging at debug/warn level), or calling it at a point where failure is unlikely (e.g., after `did-finish-load`).

`apply()` updates the Solid zoom signal before confirming `window.api.setZoomFactor()` succeeds, and then swallows any error. If the IPC call fails (e.g., window/webContents gone, handler not registered yet), the renderer state can diverge from the actual webContents zoom with no visibility. Consider either (a) awaiting the IPC call and only committing `setWebviewZoom` on success, or (b) rolling back the signal / emitting a log when the IPC call rejects so desyncs are diagnosable.

The prompt autocomplete already merges command-dialog slashes with `sync.data.command` entries and does not deduplicate them. Adding a `slash` registration here means session prompts will now show two indistinguishable `/btw` options: one from this UI command and one from the built-in command registry.

This maps every non-throwing response to text, so normal SDK error responses become a fake success message (`"No response"`) instead of surfacing the real server error. Users won't see why `/btw` failed unless this call opts into `throwOnError` or checks `res.error` explicitly.
`./dialog` does not exist in this directory, so this import breaks the TUI build. Other dialog components import the dialog context from the UI layer (`@tui/ui/dialog` / `../ui/dialog`).

This helper always calls `dialog.replace(...)` after the request settles, even if the user already dismissed the loading dialog or opened a different modal. The late response can therefore reopen the BTW overlay or clobber another dialog unexpectedly.

`BtwInput.model` is declared as a string model selector, but this branch treats it as an already-resolved `Provider.Model`, and the fallback reads `session.model!.modelID` even though session metadata stores the field as `id` and may be absent on fresh sessions. `/btw` will therefore fail when the caller supplies `model`, when there is no small-model candidate, or on sessions that do not have a stored model yet.

This hard-codes the `build` agent, but agents can be disabled or replaced via config. In setups where `build` is removed, `/btw` will always fail with `Agent not found: "build"` even though another primary/default agent is available.

This logs the full side-question text at info level. Unlike the normal prompt/shell paths, that sends arbitrary user content to server logs, which creates an unnecessary data-exposure path for potentially sensitive questions.

Registering `btw` as a normal built-in command advertises it through `GET /command`, but `SessionPrompt.command()` still executes listed commands as persisted conversation turns. Any client that drives slash commands via the public command API will get the opposite of the documented `/btw` behavior unless it reimplements the TUI's special-case handling.

By the time this branch runs, home prompts have already called `session.create()` above to obtain a `sessionID`. Submitting `/btw ...` from the home screen therefore creates and navigates to an empty session even though the feature is supposed to be ephemeral and not add anything to the conversation.

This has the same error-swallowing problem as the prompt intercept: SDK responses that contain `error` but do not throw are converted into `"No response"`, so the dialog hides the actual failure reason from the user.

Suggestion: same ASCII style note here: this new comment introduces a Unicode arrow. Consider `weakest to strongest` or `weakest -> strongest`.

Suggestion: this new test file introduces several `any`s (the captured body, fetch parameters, mock model, and providerOptions). The style guide asks us to avoid `any` when a narrower type is practical; a small shape for the captured gateway body plus `Parameters<typeof fetch>` / `unknown` for parsed JSON would keep the regression test type-safe without much extra code.

Suggestion: the style guide says to default to ASCII when editing or creating files. This new file introduces an em dash here and Unicode arrows below; consider ASCII `-` / `->` unless the Unicode punctuation is intentional.

Suggestion: consider keeping `other` terminal in this outer-loop guard unless there are tool calls to send back. `hasToolCalls` already prevents exiting after client-side MCP/tool calls, but adding `other` here also continues when a provider returns an unmapped finish reason with no tool calls. Since `SessionProcessor.process()` returns `continue` for a successful stream and relies on this next iteration to stop, that case can create extra assistant turns instead of ending on the provider response.

`store.recovered` is never reset, so after the first `onConnectError` triggers a clone, any later connect errors (even for other tabs or after switching sessions/servers) will be ignored and the terminal may get stuck. Consider tracking recovery attempts per PTY id (e.g., a Set of ids) and/or resetting the flag when a terminal successfully connects or when the active PTY changes; also consider resetting on clone failure so a single transient error doesn’t permanently disable recovery.

`loadWorkspace` uses a default parameter `serverScope = scope()`. When callers pass `undefined` explicitly (e.g., `prev.scope` when the previous scope was local), the default kicks in and uses the *current* scope, so cache/persist lookups may target the wrong scope. Make `serverScope` an explicit argument (no default) and always pass the intended scope value from call sites.

This effect intends to trim the *previous* workspace’s terminal buffers when dir/id/scope changes, but `loadWorkspace(prev.dir, prev.id, prev.scope)` can resolve to the current scope when `prev.scope` is `undefined` (due to `loadWorkspace`’s default param). This can trim the wrong terminal store and leave the old one untrimmed.

Terminal persistence is now written under `terminal:${scope}` for non-local servers, but `clearWorkspaceTerminals` still only clears the unscoped `terminal` key/cache entry. This means resetting a workspace may leave scoped terminal state behind. Consider updating `clearWorkspaceTerminals` to accept a scope (or clear the current scope via server context) and remove the corresponding persisted key(s)/cache entries.

The fallback for unsupported `pty.connectToken` is gated on `password` being truthy. For same-origin/local connections where no password is set, a 404/405 or "Request is not supported" will still fail the whole connect flow even though the websocket may work without a ticket. Consider treating these "unsupported" cases as "no ticket" at least when `sameOrigin` is true (or unconditionally), so legacy servers can still connect.

`api.addServer()` returns as soon as the controller queues `startServer()`, but this lookup only searches the ready server list. Because WSL entries are added to `items()` only after `runtime.kind === "ready"`, `conn` is always `undefined` here and the wizard never auto-selects the server it just added.
The built-in local sidecar now gets the overflow-menu trigger too, but every menu item below is still guarded off for non-HTTP/non-WSL rows. That leaves an empty menu button on the Local Server row.

`opencodeReady()` treats a known desktop/version mismatch as ready, so `allReady()` becomes true and the Add WSL Server button is enabled even when `matchesDesktop === false`. That lets users add/start a server the UI already knows is on an incompatible version.

When `pendingRestart` is true the machine itself needs a Windows reboot, but this button only relaunches OpenCode. Clicking it cannot clear the condition and sends the user back into the same blocked state.

Installed distro names can contain spaces (the parser above accepts them, and imported/custom distros often do), but `openWslTerminal` rejects anything outside `[A-Za-z0-9_.-]`. That makes the Open terminal action fail for valid distros such as `Ubuntu Preview` or custom imported names.

Updating or reinstalling OpenCode only changes the files on disk; it never restarts an already running WSL sidecar. After this completes, the UI will report the new version from `opencode --version`, but requests still hit the old in-memory server process until the user manually restarts it.

Only `runtime.kind === "ready"` WSL servers are passed into `AppInterface`. If the active WSL sidecar later moves to `failed` or `stopped`, its entry disappears from `ServerProvider` and the app falls back to the base sidecar instead of surfacing that the selected backend went away.

Server switching now depends on callers supplying `onNavigateHome`, but existing entry points such as the status popover still open this dialog without that prop. In those paths the app no longer navigates back to `/` before changing backends, so it can stay on a stale `/:dir` route that only existed on the previous server.

For `\\wsl$` / `\\wsl.localhost` inputs this drops the source distro name and returns only `/${subpath}`. If the user picks a folder from a different distro than the active one, the app silently opens the same subpath in the current distro instead of rejecting the selection.

This publishes `state.active`, not the server returned by `current()`. When the active key disappears from `allServers()` (for example after a WSL sidecar drops out and `current()` falls back to the base sidecar), `window.__OPENCODE__.activeServer` stays on the stale `wsl:*` key, so the Electron platform layer keeps doing WSL path translation even though the UI has already fallen back to the local server.

This strips the distro name from `\\wsl$\<distro>\...` paths without verifying that it matches the requested distro. If a user picks a file from a different distro than the active server, the code will silently return the same `/...` path inside the active distro instead, which can open or save the wrong file.

WSL distro names are not limited to `[a-zA-Z0-9_.-]` — imported/custom distros can contain spaces. The rest of this module already passes distro names as separate argv entries, so this validation will reject legitimate distros in the onboarding flow's “Open terminal” action even though `wsl.exe -d <name>` can launch them.

`allReady()` treats any installed `opencode` binary as ready, even when `matchesDesktop === false`. That means the wizard still enables “Add WSL server” for a version-mismatched distro even though the UI is telling the user to update it first, which defeats the compatibility check this flow just performed.

This new dialog hardcodes user-facing English strings instead of routing them through `language.t(...)` like the existing dialogs (for example `dialog-edit-project.tsx` and `dialog-select-server.tsx`). As written, the entire WSL onboarding flow will ship untranslated in every non-English locale.

`DialogSelectServer` now relies on `onNavigateHome` to leave the current `/:dir/...` route before switching servers, but this call site still opens it without that prop. Selecting a different server from “Manage servers” while you are inside a project/session route will therefore remount the app against the new backend on the old path instead of returning to `/` first.

This dialog also introduces new user-facing labels as hardcoded English (`"Add WSL server"`, `"Add WSL"`, `"Retry start"`, `"Install OpenCode"`, etc.) instead of using the existing i18n pattern with `language.t(...)`. Even if the wizard itself is localized, the surrounding server-management UI will still be untranslated for non-English locales.

The menu trigger is now rendered for every `sidecar`, but the local desktop sidecar does not satisfy any of the menu item conditions below. That leaves the built-in Local Server with a clickable overflow button that opens an empty menu.

`spawn_command` still accepts a single shell-style `args` string, but this branch now re-tokenizes it with `split_whitespace()`. That changes the API contract compared with the nushell path and the previous Unix behavior: any argument that is quoted or contains spaces will now be split incorrectly on non-nushell Unix systems, so command construction becomes shell-dependent.

This new shell-selection path is not covered by tests. The file already has unit tests for the helper functions below, but nothing exercises `spawn_command`, so regressions in the non-nushell direct-launch path or the preserved nushell wrapper path would not be caught automatically.

Enabling Chromium remote debugging even in non-packaged builds is a security-sensitive default. Consider (1) explicitly binding to loopback by also setting `remote-debugging-address=127.0.0.1` so it can’t accidentally listen on external interfaces if defaults change, and (2) not hard-coding `9222` (port collisions are common) — e.g., make it configurable via env/CLI and/or respect an existing `--remote-debugging-port` by checking `app.commandLine.hasSwitch()` before appending.

Consider adding a regression assertion in `packages/opencode/test/server/httpapi-bridge.test.ts` (or similar) that the transformed OpenAPI schema for `POST /experimental/workspace/warp` has `requestBody.application/json.schema.properties.id` nullable (e.g., `anyOf` includes `{type:"null"}`). The existing request-body parity test only checks the high-level "object" kind and won’t catch this nullability regression.

`applyZoom` updates `requestedZoom` immediately, but if `window.api.setZoomFactor(next)` rejects (IPC failure, destroyed webContents, etc.), `requestedZoom` will stay out of sync with the real zoom factor and subsequent +/- steps will compound from a value that never applied. Consider adding a `.catch(...)` path that restores `requestedZoom` (e.g., to `webviewZoom()` or `await window.api.getZoomFactor()`) and avoids leaving state inconsistent.

`minHeight` previously used `40 / zoom()` on macOS (keeping the titlebar’s *physical* height stable when zooming in/out). The new formula `titlebarHeight / Math.min(titlebarZoom(), 1)` no longer compensates for zoom-in on macOS, so the macOS titlebar will grow taller as zoom increases. If the intent is Windows-only behavior, consider keeping the prior macOS calculation (or otherwise ensuring macOS remains stable at zoom > 1).

Adding `viewport-fit=cover` exposes the unsafe areas for every fixed/overlay surface, but this change only pads `#root`. User-visible overlays such as the mobile sidebar (`packages/app/src/pages/layout.tsx:2416-2428`), dialogs (`packages/ui/src/components/dialog.css:10-29`), and toasts (`packages/ui/src/components/toast.css:1-10`) are all still positioned against the raw viewport, so they can continue to overlap the notch/home-indicator on iOS/iPadOS.

Padding `#root` does not help the app states that still render full-viewport children (`packages/app/src/app.tsx:203-205`, `251-252`, and `packages/app/src/pages/error.tsx:258-259`). Those `h-dvh`/`w-screen` wrappers will overflow the padded root once `viewport-fit=cover` is enabled, so the loading/connection/error screens can still extend into the unsafe area.

This doesn’t fully match the PR summary claim that loopback is kept in `NO_PROXY`: `ensureLoopbackNoProxy()` runs here, but later `spawnLocalServer()` calls `prepareServerEnv()` which does `Object.assign(process.env, { ...process.env, ...shellEnv, ... })`. If `shellEnv` contains `NO_PROXY`/`no_proxy` without loopback entries, it will overwrite the earlier upsert and loopback may no longer be exempted for subsequent reads of `process.env`. Consider applying the loopback upsert after merging `shellEnv` (e.g., inside `prepareServerEnv()` or immediately after it) so the final environment always retains the loopback exclusions.

`prepareServerEnv(password)` is called after `needsMigration = !sqliteFileExists()` and after `getSidecarPort()` has already read `process.env.OPENCODE_PORT`. Since `prepareServerEnv` merges the user shell env into `process.env` (including potentially `XDG_DATA_HOME`, `OPENCODE_PORT`, proxy vars, etc.), Desktop can make migration/port decisions using a different environment than the embedded server import will later observe (xdg-basedir reads env at import time). Consider generating `password` and calling `prepareServerEnv` at the very start of `initialize()` (before `sqliteFileExists()` / `getSidecarPort()`), so both Desktop and the embedded server agree on the effective environment.

`DEFAULT_CSP` is now just `csp()` and appears to be unused anywhere in the repo (no imports/usages found). Consider removing this export to avoid keeping a dead constant around, or add a brief comment explaining why it remains part of the module API.

Fixed in kkugot/opencode@43b779727. The outer loop now treats `other` as terminal unless the assistant message has client-side tool calls via `hasToolCalls`, so unmapped finish reasons without tool work do not trigger an extra assistant turn. Added a regression test for that case.

Switching this bootstrap step from `ensureQueryData` to `fetchQuery` will refetch `/app/agents` on every bootstrap because the query has no `staleTime`. That defeats the cache reuse this PR is aiming for and can add duplicate network traffic whenever a workspace is reopened or re-bootstrapped.

Using `fetchQuery` here forces a fresh `path.get()` request whenever this branch runs, since the query is stale immediately by default. The previous `ensureQueryData` path could reuse cached path data, so this change can introduce unnecessary bootstrap round-trips for every workspace.

This loading selector still uses the project root worktree as the query key, but `loadMore()` and the child store operate on `props.directory`. For sandbox workspaces (`project.sandboxes`), the session fetch runs under `[sandbox, "loadSessions"]`, so this component will never show its loading state while that sandbox is fetching.

This still misses the keyed path. `needle` is NFC, but `fuzzysort` reads raw values from `filterKeys`, so an NFD Korean path returned by file search can get wrapped as `title` and filtered out again. dumb fix: normalize the keyed values too, or make callers use a normalized search key.

This startup wait needs a timeout. As written, the desktop can hang forever if the sidecar stalls before posting `ready`/`error` (module import, sqlite migration, native binding load, `Server.listen`). The 30s health timeout in `index.ts` starts only after `spawnLocalServer()` resolves, so it does not cover this phase. VS Code wraps utility-process connection and ready/initialized handshakes with explicit 60s timeouts (`localProcessExtensionHost.ts` around its connect and handshake paths). Please race `ready`/`error`/`exit` with a startup timeout and kill the utility process on timeout.

This startup error path posts the error but leaves the utility process alive. The parent rejects, but nothing guarantees this sidecar exits or gets killed. VS Code treats utility-process exit/crash as lifecycle state and cleans up process state immediately. Please `process.exit(1)` after posting the startup error, and have the parent kill on rejected startup as a backup.

Shutdown is fire-and-forget here. Callers like relaunch/update/quit immediately continue, so this 2s force-kill timer may never fire if Electron main exits first. VS Code has `waitForExit(maxWaitTimeMs)` that waits for exit, then force kills, and `WindowUtilityProcess` wires that into window lifecycle grace time. Please make `SidecarListener.stop()` return a `Promise<void>` that waits for `stopped` or `exit`, then kills after a grace period; then await it in relaunch/update paths where possible.

This passes the live mutable `process.env` object directly. VS Code's utility-process wrapper clones env, applies explicit process metadata, removes dangerous env vars, handles platform-specific env adjustments, and stringifies every value before spawn (`utilityProcess.ts:createEnv`). We should create a fresh env object here, apply only the sidecar values we need, sanitize if possible, and ensure all values are strings rather than passing `process.env` by reference.
